## The Rarest Day

**February 29, 1960 — a Monday.**

You share your exact birthday with roughly one in every 1,461 people — those born on the day the calendar inserts to keep itself honest with the sun. In 66 years of life, February 29 has arrived 16 times for you. The next one comes in 2028, when you'll turn 68 on your 17th real birthday. This is not merely a calendar curiosity. It means you have spent your entire life watching time move differently than it does for almost everyone else — a small, recurring reminder that the systems humans use to measure the world are conventions, not facts.

The world itself seemed to be reckoning with that idea on the day you arrived.

---

**The earth moved that night.**

On February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck the Moroccan coastal city of Agadir at roughly midnight — the worst possible hour, when the city was asleep inside its buildings. The quake lasted fifteen seconds. When it was over, Agadir was largely rubble. Between 12,000 and 15,000 people were killed — approximately a third of the city's entire population, erased in a quarter of a minute. You were born into a world that had just experienced one of the deadliest earthquakes in African history, on the exact day you entered it. The Agadir earthquake reshaped Morocco's relationship with urban planning, disaster preparedness, and the physical fragility of built environments in ways that echo into modern city design across the developing world.

---

**The sit-ins had started four weeks earlier.**

On February 1, 1960 — 28 days before your birthday — four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, ordered coffee, and refused to leave when they were denied service. By the time you were born, the sit-in movement had spread to dozens of cities across the South. February 1960 was the month the Civil Rights Movement became impossible to contain within any single strategy or leader or location. It was a spontaneous, decentralized uprising happening in real time, and it was still spreading on the day you were born. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee would form six weeks later. The world you arrived into was in the middle of one of the most significant moral reckonings in American history.

---

**±30 Days — Sharpeville**

*Twenty-one days after you were born*, on March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters in the township of Sharpeville who had gathered to demonstrate against the pass laws requiring Black South Africans to carry identification documents at all times. Sixty-nine people were killed; most were shot in the back as they fled. The Sharpeville massacre changed the global calculus around apartheid: it galvanized the international anti-apartheid movement, prompted South Africa's eventual expulsion from the Commonwealth, and marked the moment when the African National Congress shifted toward armed resistance. Nelson Mandela would be imprisoned four years later and not released for another 27 years — 1990, when you were 30. The arc from Sharpeville to Mandela's release runs almost exactly the length of your childhood and young adulthood.

---

**1960 was the Year of Africa.**

The year you were born, seventeen African nations gained independence from European colonial powers — Cameroon, Togo, Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Somalia, Benin, Niger, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville, Gabon, Senegal, Mali, Nigeria, and Mauritania. The European colonial project, which had organized the world's maps since the 1880s, was collapsing. The decolonization happening in Africa, the Suez humiliation four years earlier, the sit-ins happening in American streets — these were all the same story told in different languages: the political arrangements of the nineteenth century were not going to survive the twentieth.

---

**Your childhood was the Kennedy decade.**

You were three when John Kennedy was shot in Dallas — old enough to absorb the shock in the adults around you, too young to process it as history. The 1960s were the backdrop of your entire childhood: the Civil Rights Act when you were four, the Voting Rights Act at five, Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination and Robert Kennedy's assassination both in 1968, when you were eight. The moon landing was July 1969 — you were nine, and it was summer, and it was the kind of thing a nine-year-old holds onto for life. You came of age during one of the most compressed and violent decades of American political history, old enough to feel it, young enough to be shaped by it rather than merely witnessed by it.

---

**Vietnam was your generation's shadow.**

The draft ended in January 1973, when you were twelve — just before you'd have been old enough to be threatened by it. But Vietnam defined the generation immediately ahead of you, the older brothers and cousins and neighbors, and its aftermath — the bitterness, the distrust of institutions, the moral complexity that didn't resolve neatly — was the cultural atmosphere of your adolescence. Watergate happened when you were thirteen and fourteen. You were fifteen when Nixon resigned. By the time you were old enough to vote, the country had spent a decade demonstrating that the adults in charge were frequently wrong, sometimes catastrophically.

---

**The walls came down when you were twenty-nine.**

The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, when you were thirty-one. The existential threat that had organized your entire childhood — the one behind the duck-and-cover drills, the nuclear arsenals, the Cuban Missile Crisis you were two years old for — simply ended. Nothing replaced it cleanly. The 1990s were prosperous and strange, a decade that felt like an intermission between one era and whatever came next. September 11, 2001 announced what came next, when you were 41.

---

**The synthesis.**

You were born on a day the calendar only admits four times per decade, into a year when the world's political architecture was actively reorganizing itself — decolonization in Africa, direct action in American streets, earthquake rubble in Morocco, the Cold War hardening into its long frozen middle. The particular quality of 1960 is that everything felt simultaneously fragile and urgent: the old arrangements were visibly failing and the new ones weren't yet formed.

Sixty-six years later, you have watched that pattern repeat — the fragile arrangements, the urgent moments, the sense that the world is reorganizing itself again — often enough to know that it doesn't stop. The calendar will offer you February 29 again in 2028. The world will be different by then. It always is.
